title: Ithilrûnë Ailinor
imageAlt: Portrait of Ithilrûnë, a scholar and seeker of knowledge
imageCaption: Ithilrûnë — scholar, seeker, and preserver of choice.
dek: A researcher whose commitment to memory and independent judgment meets its hardest test when understanding itself fails.

facts.Crisis: The Chain and Maw resist understanding
facts.Growth: Admits ignorance and revises her Chain theory after further observation
facts.Risk: Decisive action may become preferable to uncertainty

body:
Ithilrûnë is a powerful, cunning magical researcher whose confidence rests on understanding systems well enough to preserve options. Raw power matters, but knowledge creates leverage: observe the rules, find the pressure point, and keep danger from becoming fate. Her principle is not abstract scholarship. Knowledge preserves choice.

That principle also explains why ignorance wounds her so deeply. A danger she understands can be planned around. Powerlessness can be endured if its mechanism can be named. What destabilizes Ithilrûnë is evidence that refuses to become a coherent model, because the loss of understanding also removes the means through which she normally protects herself and other people.

The Plains of Trial: grief as a competence problem

After Sildithas dies in the Plains of Trial and returns only hours later, Ithilrûnë says she could have prevented it and calls the failure unacceptable. Pain becomes a problem of insufficient knowledge and preparation: she should have known more, planned better, or acted sooner.

She answers the loss by asking what she should have known or prepared differently. That self-reproach is part of the account. Whether different preparation would have prevented the death is a separate question the record does not settle. She puts responsibility on herself even where the causes and alternatives remain uncertain.

The Shadow Roads: knowledge and authority

The tear in reality is almost designed to test her. Where others see an unknown danger, Ithilrûnë sees offered knowledge: an explanation of the world, perhaps new lands, and therefore new choices. She votes to enter.

Her flaw appears when she calls refusal cowardice. A personal compulsion to know becomes a judgment about what everyone else must risk. Ithilrûnë is strongest when understanding enlarges another person’s choices and most dangerous when it convinces her that she should decide which choices are legitimate.

The Chain and Maw crisis

By the September 2026 Chain/Maw crisis, Ithilrûnë is unkempt, listless, distracted, and irritable. Voraketh has attacked the foundation of her normal competence. A Delerium chain suppresses her magical strength and dangerous constructs defend or repair it; the Maw consumes magic with frightening ease. The force within may be an artifact, a prison, or both.

One figure appears associated with the Maw and another may be watching. The primary recent spelling Deyara Thorn has been recovered, with Derya Thorne preserved as an older variant, but Ithilrûnë cannot connect the name reliably to an identity, allegiance, or history. She cannot determine whether the associated figure is victim, enemy, god, eldritch danger, or evidence of a divine mistake. Each possibility changes the morality of intervention, and the evidence cannot yet distinguish among them.

The broken sequence: Ithilrûnë normally moves from observation to understanding, manipulation, and preserved choice. The Maw stops the sequence at understanding.

“I know fucking nothing. I hate it.”

The admission is more than frustration at an unsolved objective. Ithilrûnë’s usual source of safety, value, and care is failing in public. She can generate explanations—Talan may be concealing a mistake, Talan and Physisia may be in conflict, a mortal may have angered him, or the prisoner may truly be too dangerous to release—but she cannot responsibly rank them. The Codex preserves every one as theory.

Creating an actionable problem

Uncertainty does not make Ithilrûnë passive. It makes her desperate to recover agency. She wants to break the Chain and extract the figure. She considers Scribonia’s research, Draygar’s overwhelming force, additional Vanguard involvement, and more warriors like Pappy. She even proposes acquiring ancient null-magic armor and entering the Maw herself.

She knows the plan is reckless. She chooses the risk in an attempt to act on an unknown she finds intolerable. The Chain also offends her morally. Sleeping beside it feels diminishing; leaving it untouched feels profane or sacrilegious even though she is not conventionally devout.

The moment Ithilrûnë follows

Ithilrûnë is socially skilled and accustomed to steering conversations toward answers she already sees. At the end of the Maw conversation, she does something different. Sildithas admits that his own theology has become unstable and returns to his oath rather than pretending to possess a solution. He proposes a feast so the people still facing the Maw can share some joy while its questions remain unanswered.

Ithilrûnë calls this a different form of wisdom. Because her own has not moved them forward, she agrees to follow his lead. She does not reject knowledge or cunning. She accepts that wisdom can remain real even when it is not hers.

Relationships as leverage—and trust

Sildithas is her clearest intellectual and temperamental counterweight. Their teasing rests on real trust, and she follows when his ethical method succeeds where analysis has stalled. Coralyn is a major magical ally whose reluctance at the Shadow Roads exposes Ithilrûnë’s tendency to moralize risk. Pappy can shield fragile casters as a physical defender. Ithilrûnë can call Scribonia a “piss-ant” while still judging him the researcher most likely to help, and she considers Draygar useful because the island has made finesse unreliable.

A more difficult form of wisdom

Her current movement is competence through knowledge → radical uncertainty → escalating attempts to recover agency → admission of ignorance → willingness to borrow another person’s wisdom. The arc is not “knowledge is bad.” It asks whether Ithilrûnë can keep investigating without making decisive danger preferable to responsible uncertainty.

What remains unresolved

The archive identifies the island as Voraketh and dates the crisis to September 2026, but it does not yet know the exact day, what the Maw is, who is associated with it, who may be watching, who Deyara Thorn is, why Talan originally made the Chains, why Physisia says they became a curse, whether they can be altered safely, or whether the proposed feast takes place.

Raw chaos and the Grove

Ithilrûnë identifies a mote as raw chaos. Sildithas relays her theory that order and chaos have been forcibly separated in Voraketh. The tree at the Last Grove absorbs returned motes, but their precise role in restoring Physisia or the forest remains unresolved.

December 2024 · a gift of memory

Ithilrûnë offers pipes of remembrance to people she describes as valuing memory and knowledge. The scene preserves respectful participation in a Rahu ceremony alongside her later distrust. Her political position is not an unchanging reaction to a culture she never encountered.

Distrust is a position, not a consensus

Her later judgments of the Rahu are severe. They belong to her interpretation of danger, not an objective description of every Rahu person or a verdict shared by all Pristinians. The Codex retains the disagreement alongside other people’s negotiations and friendships.

In October she demands transparency before obedience and punctuates the challenge with a joke about her dresses. The humor keeps the principle attached to a person: she can contest a direction without becoming a generic voice of solemn dissent.

Protecting what makes a person themselves

In February 2025 she warns a party about a being that she says can steal a husk and devour who and what a person is. The warning establishes her stated understanding of the threat. It does not identify the being conclusively or explain every use of the word husk across the setting.

A June research exchange asks for meaning rather than merely recognizing an object. Knowledge matters to her because interpretation makes action possible. The earlier scenes deepen the later Chain and Maw crisis already recorded here; they do not replace her admission of ignorance or her willingness to follow Sildithas’s different wisdom.

Recorded scenes

Dates refer to transcript postings.

  • 22 December 2024 · pipes of remembrance
  • 15 February 2025 · the identity warning
  • 27 October · transparency and humor
  • 9 June 2026 · seeking meaning

Care and the demand for decisive action

Ithilrûnë helps investigate Murr’s infernal sickness, yet argues that treating each local danger only delays the island’s deeper crisis. She goes toward the Chains with Carmen and Paco while the others confront the blight. Her belief that pain marks a path to freeing someone remains a belief, not a narrator-confirmed solution.

The intervening Chain encounter is absent here. She is later witnessed alive, and Carmen refers to having saved her. The excerpt does not establish a death, resurrection or a complete account of that rescue.

Scene references: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.

Revising the model without resolving the mystery

In the next quest she tests the Chains by whispering a name and looking for a response. Small movements and markings give her more to interpret, but she explicitly admits that her earlier explanation was wrong. She now thinks the Chains constrain the Maw and that releasing whoever she believes is inside may allow another answer.

She changes her mind, but the markings do not by themselves establish who made the Chains or identify anyone at the Maw’s center. Her explanation remains a theory.

She prefers a final attempt with no escape visible, while Carmen warns that the war needs living companions. Ithilrûnë nevertheless proposes returning to camp to think. Neither her proposed release nor its feared consequences has occurred in this record.

Scene references: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.

At the Grove · impatience and hands-on help

The spores make Ithilrûnë cough, and she complains that dying of a cough would be an indignity. Her response to the others is abrasive. She dismisses Pappy’s honored mushroom cap as a need to wash his hair, questions why Coralyn brought Alfred back, and tells her to stop crying and fix the mistake. Pappy eventually tells her to be quiet while he studies the blight.

She wants the company to face the Maw rather than spend its strength on smaller problems. Yet the same record puts her hands in Murr’s matted fur as she reaches for the corruption within. The narrator distinguishes that corruption as infernal, rather than delerium. Sildithas’s touch supplies strength, and Murr rises.

Her impatience with the company and her part in helping the wolf both belong in the scene. The successful help does not make her earlier words gentle, and it does not settle her argument that the deeper crisis should come first.

Saving power, admitting she needs company

Back at camp, Ithilrûnë asks whether the next constructs should be fought or bypassed. She wants to reserve her power for the Maw, and says she will be little more than a pretty face if the company spends its strength too soon. Carmen answers with an unflattering reminder of having rescued her.

Ithilrûnë admits she needs help and hates needing it. She describes being slow without her magic and warns that worse constructs lie ahead. When Carmen teases her for learning to rain fireballs and thinking herself untouchable, she starts to correct the technical description, then stops because Carmen probably does not care. Pappy offers wine after reminding her that he warned her.

The exchange records her account and her companions’ recollections of the preceding danger. It does not supply the missing fight as a witnessed death or resurrection. Their immediate problem is how to travel together without using up the power she wants for what comes next.

Stopping the axes and choosing to go farther

Ithilrûnë answered the gongs before everyone had finished eating. Her flight and Sildithas’s mount brought them to the Chain ahead of Pappy and Coralyn. Two constructs were hacking it with axes. She recognized their kind, but recognition did not establish a controller or the order behind this attack.

Her necrotic meteors struck the attackers and the Chain. The resulting force knocked companions down, part of the cost of her decisive response. She destroyed the second construct; the narrator established both were down. Coralyn later healed her wounds. At the boundary, magic remained suppressed despite severe weakening and necrotic contamination. Ithilrûnë proposed a common force behind the plague and machines, without confirmation of that connection.

She urged the company onward toward the Maw. Freedom of Movement and telekinesis protected her footing for a time, but after an hour the spell ended and the pull took hold again. Coralyn’s memory also changed. Ithilrûnë’s decision had carried them beyond the fight without yet bringing them to an answer or a safe return. Read the attack and unfinished journey →

profile.personality: Ithilrûnë seeks knowledge because informed people possess more meaningful choices. She is intellectually confident but not incapable of humility: when the Maw defeats her model, she admits what she does not know and accepts another person’s wisdom without pretending that uncertainty has ended the inquiry.
profile.achievements: A researcher whose commitment to memory and independent judgment meets its hardest test when understanding itself fails.
profile.relationships: Sildithas is her clearest philosophical counterpart. When analysis reaches its limit, his proposal of fellowship and a feast offers a different form of wisdom, and Ithilrûnë chooses to follow without surrendering her identity as a scholar. Coralyn, Carmen, St. Anky, Brianna, and Ghilsen widen that relationship into a company joined by danger and incomplete knowledge.
